summary.text: 鸡 is the simplified character for 雞, “chicken.” The early 雞 graph is interpreted as a picture of a chicken, later supplemented with sound-bearing 奚 and a bird element. Its first reported oracle-bone use is as a place name, so the earliest meaning is not certain.

formation.text: The historical formation of 雞 is best described as a development from a pictograph to a phonosemantic compound: early forms are interpreted as depicting a chicken, and later forms combine 奚 as a phonetic with a bird element, 隹 or 鳥. Modern 鸡 is a simplified character related to 雞 through the attested form 鳮; its visible 又 is not evidence for a historical 又 + 鸟 construction.

components.text: In the early 雞 pictograph, the whole graph is interpreted as a chicken, with the head, crest and open beak emphasized. This is a whole-picture analysis, not a decomposition into its modern strokes; the earliest reported oracle use is as a place name, leaving the picture’s original referent uncertain.

In 雞, 奚 supplies a sound cue rather than its independent lexical meaning. Shuowen explicitly identifies it as phonetic. Mandarin 奚 xī and 雞 jī differ today; the dossier’s Middle Chinese forms, hej and kej, share a rhyme but differ in initial, while its Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese comparison is approximate and not independently verified at the dataset publisher.

sound_limitation.text: The reported Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese comparison is an unverified local data cross-check, and the inspected sources do not establish identical reconstructed readings. The phonetic role itself is supported by the historical dictionary’s explicit analysis.

sound.text: The component and character share the Middle Chinese rhyme in the supplied categories, but have different initials; their modern Mandarin readings also differ. The Old Chinese comparison is approximate and is not treated as an exact match.
sound.system: Middle Chinese categories and Mandarin; Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese comparison *[g]ˤe vs *kˤe is approximate and locally cross-checked, not externally verified

components.text: 隹 is the bird element in the Qin and later form of 雞. The written record also has 鳥 forms in some Warring States Qi and Chu materials; Shuowen calls 鷄 a Zhou-script form written with 鳥. The evidence does not support a simple sequence in which 鳥 was only a later substitute for 隹.

鳮 is an attested simplified-style variant associated with 雞 and is listed in the 1956 simplification scheme. The modern standardized 鸡 is related to 雞 through the simplification record, but the exact graphic route from 鳮 to 鸡 is not fully documented here; 又 should not be assigned a historical role in 雞.

history.text: The curated oracle-script image is a modern redraw of a form interpreted as a chicken picture, not an ancient artifact image. The reported earliest oracle-bone use is a place name; a later account describes 奚 as added to distinguish the graph from other bird pictures. These accounts support a pictograph-to-compound interpretation, but do not establish a fully dated sequence or the first meaning.

The bird element varies across the record: some Warring States Qi and Chu forms use 鳥, while Qin forms and later writing use 隹. Shuowen describes 鷄 as a Zhou-script form from 鳥, and later variant records treat 鷄 and 雞 as equivalent forms. The evidence does not establish one simple linear path between the forms.

The 1956 scheme associates the simplified spelling 鸡 with 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟. It does not establish that 鸡 arose by replacing 奚 with 又, so the modern strokes should not be read as proof of that component history.

uncertainties.text: The sources interpret early 雞 as a chicken picture, but the earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place name. The exact original referent, earliest lexical meaning and chronology of the shift to the phonosemantic form remain uncertain.
The record varies between 鳥 and 隹 as the bird element across script traditions and periods. It does not establish a complete sequence or show that 鳥 was only a later replacement.
The simplified-character evidence connects 鸡 with 鳮（雞）, but does not document the precise steps by which the standardized form took its modern shape.

senses.text: A Qin bamboo-slip passage is reported using 雞 for chicken. The oracle-bone place-name use does not by itself establish that this animal sense was the graph’s earliest meaning.

senses.period: oracle-bone script tradition; exact dating unresolved
senses.text: An oracle-bone use of 雞 is reported as a place name. This attests a use of the graph, but does not establish the name’s referent or the graph’s original lexical meaning.

senses.gloss: 谿, valley or stream, written with 雞
senses.period: Mawangdui manuscript witness; exact borrowing date unresolved
senses.text: In a Mawangdui text, 雞 is reported as a phonetic loan for 谿, “valley/stream”; another manuscript copy has 溪. This is graph reuse for a different word, not a meaning development from “chicken.” The source report gives no contemporary sound values or demonstrated sound rationale, so the proposed sound-based mechanism remains incompletely established.
The common current meaning is chicken; the dossier supplies modern dictionary glosses and readings.

limitations.text: The reported oracle-bone place-name use and Qin-slip animal use do not establish a direct semantic transition between them or identify the pictograph’s earliest lexical value.
The reported Mawangdui loan lacks contemporary pronunciations and a demonstrated phonological rationale; its exact motivation and timing remain unresolved.

overview.text: 雞, now written 鸡 in simplified Chinese, means “chicken.” Its older form began as a picture interpreted as a chicken and developed into a compound with a sound cue and a bird element; the earliest reported use is a place name.

components.text: Early forms are interpreted as a picture of a chicken. The whole graph is the picture; its first reported use as a place name leaves the original referent uncertain.
奚 contributes sound in 雞, not its separate meaning. Its modern reading differs from 雞; the historical comparison shares a rhyme but has different initials, and the Old Chinese match is approximate.
隹 supplies the bird category in Qin and later forms. Other script traditions use 鳥, so the bird element’s written form varied.
鳮 is an attested simplified-style variant associated with 雞. The evidence does not establish each step to modern 鸡 or give 又 a historical role.

takeaway.text: Read 鸡 as a simplified form of 雞, not as proof that 又 means or depicts something in the character’s history.

relationships.text: In the historical compound 雞, 奚 is explicitly identified as the sound-bearing element; this role is scoped to 雞, not transferred to simplified 鸡.
隹 contributes the bird category in the Qin and later 雞 form; other traditions and periods also write the bird element as 鳥.
鳮 is recorded as a simplified-style variant associated with 雞; the evidence does not fully document its route to standardized 鸡.
The 1956 scheme associates 鸡 with 鳮（雞） and simplifies 鳥 as 鸟; it does not support analyzing 鸡 as a historical 又 + 鸟 compound.
